title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene (606272) on chromosome 17p13.2.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract attributes intermediate (late-onset juvenile/adolescent) cystinosis to compound heterozygous or homozygous CTNS mutations.

checks.claim: The CTNS gene is located on chromosome 17p13.2.
checks.explanation: not supported by any of the 2 cited papers. Only the abstract was supplied, and it does not give the chromosomal location of CTNS (17p13.2).

paragraphs.text: Late-onset cystinosis is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Langman et al. (1985) reported the disorder in a sibship. Thoene et al. (1999) found that patients with intermediate cystinosis were either homozygous for a mild CTNS mutation or carried a mild mutation together with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis.

paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) studied 6 patients with intermediate cystinosis and identified mutations in the CTNS gene. The disease was caused either by one mild mutation combined with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or by homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation. Two of the patients had new mutations that had not been described before. Thoene et al. (1999) transfected cystinotic fibroblasts with either normal CTNS cDNA or a cDNA carrying a mutation that causes intermediate cystinosis. Both constructs partially corrected the phenotype of the cells.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) found 23 different CTNS mutations in patients with cystinosis, 14 of them novel. In 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis, the mutations affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin. Three patients had onset before 7 years of age and a milder course than the infantile nephropathic form, and they carried missense mutations.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) studied 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Twelve had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions predicted to disrupt transmembrane domains of cystinosin. In contrast, the mutations in 2 late-onset patients affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin, which the authors stated accounted for the milder phenotype. Three patients had onset before 7 years of age but a milder course than the infantile nephropathic form. The authors suggested that the missense mutations found in these patients allow production of functional protein.
